Article Title: Colombo draw tastes like defeat as Sri Lanka dent India's WTC final hopes
Article Text:
Sri Lanka's Sonal Dinusha is congratulated by the India's team members at the end of the day five of the second cricket test match between Sri Lanka and India in Colombo, Sri Lanka, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP)

TimesofIndia.com in Colombo:

Colombo: Sri Lanka's Sonal Dinusha celebrates his hundred runs on day five of the second Test cricket match between India and Sri Lanka, in Colombo, Sri Lanka. (PTI Photo/Shailendra Bhojak)(PTI08_27_2026_000287A)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Colombo: India's Ravindra Jadeja, left, with Coach Gautam Gambhir on day five of the second Test cricket match between India and Sri Lanka, in Colombo, Sri Lanka. (PTI Photo/Shailendra Bhojak)(PTI08_27_2026_000296B)

With the handshake looming, Shubman Gill introduced himself into the attack. Judging by their body language, India had already checked out of the fixture with Sri Lanka's lead over 200 runs and little time remaining. A result in India's favour was almost out of the equation and the visitors were waiting for the formalities to be completed. Yashasvi Jaiswal was introduced from the other end, and even Dhruv Jurel rolled his arm over as the writing was on the cards. India would rue drawing a Test they were in a very good position of winning, squandering the opportunity to bolster their World Test Championship (WTC) final chances.Sometimes, draws feel like wins and Sri Lanka must have a similar feeling in Colombo. With chips down and backs to the wall, Sonal Dinusha produced a performance for the ages, who had an equally stubborn lower-order for company. He has been the rockstar for the hosts in this series and made India dance to his tunes when he battled for close to two days to eke out a hard-fought draw. The 25-year-old's sequence of scores in the series read 100, 84, 103 and 133*, and across the four innings his compact technique, composure and solid temperament stood out.It wasn't easy; whenever he came out to bat, the team was in a spot of bother and he mostly had the lower-order and tail for company. In the second Test alone, he spent nearly 147 overs out in the middle, facing 71 overs, frustrating the visitors and keeping the win out of their reach.It didn't help that Mohammed Siraj wasn't running in with the steam he would have liked and the pitch offered turn but not enough threat. The tone was set by the pair of Keshara Nuwantha and Dinusha for over 40 overs and the former ended up playing 150 deliveries in the process. Lahiru Kumara and Asitha Fernando followed the drill and India just carried on in hopes of things miraculously falling into place.The 116th over of the Sri Lankan innings was significant in more ways than one. Siraj patiently waited to bowl as Sarfaraz Khan suggested field changes to Shubman Gill before the fast bowler began. The short-ball trap was set. After trying it for two deliveries, which Sonal Dinusha ducked safely, the bowler walked up to the stumps and flipped the bails. This was India's second attempt, followed by a very creative field setting, likely the first of its kind that day.The entire field moved towards the off-side, placing enough men in catching positions for a miscued drive. Dinusha had been pushed back for most of the over and here Siraj was trying to induce a false shot from the most consistent batter of the series. The plan didn't work but India's attempt to finally make things happen brought success when Prabath Jayasuriya was dismissed in the very next over while driving against Ravindra Jadeja. India, even after picking up two wickets in the first hour after Lunch, were still two wickets away from beginning their chase but that 12-ball period summed up a story of what could have, and should have, been for India in the first session.The pitch was flat, the body language was flatter and the tactics the flattest. The open fields and the focus solely on dismissing Dinusha's partner not only allowed desperation to creep in but also prevented sustained pressure, as there were easy runs available, meaning the left-hander didn't need to take risks. India were again guilty of going through the motions and the defensive ploys were baffling to say the least at a time when wickets were needed.India, however, focused on cutting off boundaries, allowing easy singles and even keeping fielders positioned for a reverse-sweep. In a Test match! It was a period where shoulders started dropping, leaving India head coach Gautam Gambhir with no option but to summon captain Gill to the change room before the lunch break.The skipper spoke to coach Gambhir and video analyst Hari Prasad Mohan when nothing was going their way in the first session. They took the new ball, tried different combinations, played around with the field, albeit defensively, but none worked. Despite being in a position of absolute control, India played catch-up. However, with the weather gods permitting and the advantage of the first-innings run cushion, they always had the best chance of securing a favourable result.Across the two innings, Sri Lanka's lower-order, apart from the usual suspect Dinusha, remained the thorn in the flesh as they collectively faced 71 overs deliveries. This will require a lot of introspection and the team needs to be tactically better for tougher shores in future. It took India 44.1 overs to wrap up the tail in the first innings, but they couldn't do that in more than 90 overs in the second. The runs were never the question but the hosts were wiping off crucial time from the fixture, hoping the dark clouds would rescue them and help force the best result: a draw.The hosts fought for a draw - a result which looked extremely unlikely. The weather allowed India a proper crack at the opposition but the resistance from Sri Lanka's lower-order not only avoided the whitewash but also dealt a major dent to India's WTC final qualification hopes. With just one win, they now have no room to slip in the remaining seven Tests - two away against New Zealand and five at home against Australia.
Article Summary: Sonal Dinusha scores century as Sri Lanka draw second Test with India in Colombo. Dinusha has been the rockstar for the hosts in this series and made India dance to his tunes. The 25-year-old's sequence of scores in the series read 100, 84, 103 and 133*.

Article Title: 'Draw not hurting like a defeat': Shubman Gill after Sri Lanka deny India 2-0 clean sweep
Article Text:
Shubman Gill (Image credit: TimesofIndia.com)

'Draw not hurting like a defeat'

Gill defends follow-on decision

'Sri Lanka played really well'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India had looked set to complete a 2-0 series sweep against Sri Lanka, but the hosts produced a stubborn fightback to force a draw in the second Test in Colombo.Sri Lanka were bowled out for 290 in their first innings after India declared on 503/9. India captain Shubman Gill then enforced the follow-on, hoping his bowlers could finish the job and seal another big win.But Sonal Dinusha had other plans.The Sri Lankan batter scored his third century of the two-match series and remained unbeaten on 133 as Sri Lanka reached 429/9 before the players shook hands for a draw.Despite missing out on a 2-0 series win, Gill said the result was not as painful as a defeat. He also praised Sri Lanka for their effort while admitting India were disappointed after aiming for another victory."Draw not hurting like a defeat… situation wise, draw was credit to them, we hoped for a win so disappointing"Gill also said the Test provided valuable lessons for him as captain."Things always don’t go as per plan, so lot of learnings for me as well as a captain. I give 10/10 for the effort and intent of everyone."India eventually finished the series with a 1-0 win after their 165-run victory in the first Test in Galle.Gill also explained why he chose to enforce the follow-on after India gained a big lead. With rain a possibility, he wanted to give India enough time to push for victory.India had taken a 213-run first-innings lead and had Sri Lanka under pressure after enforcing the follow-on.However, Dinusha once again stood between India and victory.Resuming at 229/6, Dinusha and Keshara Nuwantha put together a crucial 112-run partnership for the seventh wicket. Nuwantha made 46, while Dinusha carried his bat through the innings.India tried different approaches on a fifth-day pitch, but the conditions became increasingly difficult for the bowlers.Manav Suthar finished with 3/121 from 41 overs, while Ravindra Jadeja took 3/94 in 38.3 overs."I don’t think follow-on backfired, we fielded for over 250 overs. We were anticipating (rain), wanted to take that chance. Had we not taken and had it rained, you would have asked why no follow on."Gill admitted that Sri Lanka deserved credit for their resistance, especially over the final three days."Sri Lanka played really well. Days 3,4 and 5 - lbw and bowled was out of equation. We attacked initially but pitch became slower today. There was slow turn. Pitch became easier, we tried our best."The India captain said his team had created opportunities on the fourth day and felt the result could have been different had those chances been converted."On Day 4 we created chances, had wickets come result could’ve been different: Shubman Gill"
Article Summary: India captain Shubman Gill defends follow-on decision. 'Draw not hurting like a defeat' says Gill. India finished the series with a 1-0 win after their 165-run victory in the first Test in Galle. Sonal Dinusha scored 133 as Sri Lanka reached 429/9 in their first innings.

Article Title: Northeast's first GM, 17-year-old Mayank Chakraborty and pupil Pratitee Bordoloi become Asia's junior chess champions
Article Text:
Mayank Chakraborty and Pratitee Bordoloi (Special Arrangements)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Struggle is still going on. Same struggle, same life. Mayank Chakraborty on life since becoming a Grandmaster

NEW DELHI: Mayank Chakraborty became India's 94th Grandmaster and the first from the Northeast region last March . He is still 17. Talking to him, however, gives away very little about his age; he sounds more like a man with years of experience on his shoulders.On Tuesday, he added another feather to his cap, lifting the coveted classical title at the Asian Junior Chess Championships in Mumbai. 13-year-old Pratitee Bordoloi clinched the classical title in the girls' category on the very same day.Chakraborty is from Assam. Bordoloi is based out of Bengaluru. However, for the past three-odd months, the distance hasn't mattered much. Chakraborty has been mentoring her, and it found a fairytale moment when both of them walked away champions from the same hall that only hosted Asia's some of the best players under the age of 20."Obviously, I became the champion; that's the best thing that happened to me," Chakraborty told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction. "But also one of my students managed to become the champion. It increases my happiness."Expanding on their preparation together, he added, "I've been mentoring her for almost three to four months now, and I started it all the way in World Youth in Monte Silvano, Italy."In Italy, Bordoloi clinched silver and became India's only medallist at the 2026 FIDE World Youth Chess Championship. On Tuesday, nevertheless, it was gold, along with a WGM (Women's Grandmaster) norm, which came without much help from her mentor during the tournament."During the tournament, it was a bit difficult because he was also playing, but before the tournament he helped me, specifically in preparing openings," an elated Pratitee told this website.Coming into the tournament as the No. 1 seed, Bordoloi felt the pressure. Her mother, Pranti Dutta Bordoloi, didn't dress it up."If I tell you no pressure, I think it will be totally lie," she said. "Whenever you play as the top seed, automatically, whether you want it or not, you will be under pressure. It's like you're giving someone a one-kilo weight on their head and telling them that they have to run now, and they have to come first."Chakraborty, also the No. 1 seed, had already won the Asian Junior Rapid title once before. But classical, he made clear, is the one that actually counts."Since Classical is the actual main form where you become World Champion, it's like I prove my superiority over everyone else," he added.Further explaining what it means to get his hands on the title, the teenager added, "Rapid Championship ends in one day, and this Classical Championship is a battle for six to seven days. So more hard work, more pressure... Classical chess requires a lot of opening preparation, mental training and all this stuff which Rapid chess doesn't require. Just play. Rapid chess is just about playing."Perhaps life has not changed much since becoming a Grandmaster for Mayank, as he muttered, "Struggle is still going on. Same struggle, same life."However, amid the "struggle", he still finds the room to mentor. How? "Honestly, I'm actually very good at multitasking, so I can manage time. I have a timetable," he said with some palpable confidence. "I have a routine, and I follow it very properly. I don't waste time. I don't have any distractions like social media and et cetera. So I can just focus on my work very well."In the next five days, Chakraborty is scheduled to fly to Turkiye and then Malaysia for chess tournaments abroad. On the other hand, Pratitee and her family are content with the WGM norm and the overall outcome of the Asian Junior C'ships, as her mother concluded, "Honestly speaking, if we do as much as we can in India, it will be very less expensive for us financially."If we do the same thing outside, it will cost 10 times more money for us."
Article Summary: Mayank Chakraborty became India's 94th Grandmaster and the first from the Northeast region last March. On Tuesday, he added another feather to his cap, lifting the coveted classical title. 13-year-old Pratitee Bordoloi clinched the classical title in the girls' category on the very same day.

Article Title: IND vs SL: For first time against India, Sri Lanka do the unthinkable in Colombo
Article Text:
AFP Photo

Sri Lanka break a long follow-on jinx

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Sri Lanka saving Tests after follow-on

vs Zimbabwe, Bulawayo, 1994 — 193/4

vs England, Lord's, 2006 — 537/9

vs West Indies, Galle, 2010 — 241/4

vs India, Colombo SSC, 2026 — 429/9

Dinusha completes a remarkable series

Hundreds in both innings, second while following on

Vijay Hazare — 116 & 145 vs Australia, Adelaide, 1948

Andy Flower — 142 & 199* vs South Africa, Harare, 2001

Sonal Dinusha — 103 & 133* vs India, Colombo SSC, 2026

NEW DELHI: For the first time against India and only the fourth time overall, Sri Lanka did the unthinkable in Colombo. After being forced to follow on and facing a huge 213-run first-innings deficit, Sri Lanka fought back brilliantly to save the second Test against India on Thursday. The match ended in a draw, with India winning the two-match series 1-0.Sri Lanka had lost 24 of their previous 27 Tests after being asked to follow on. Even more strikingly, they had lost all eight such Tests against India.But in Colombo, the hosts finally broke that run.Resuming at 229/6 on the final day, Sri Lanka finished on 429/9 before the teams agreed to call off the match. Sonal Dinusha led the resistance with an unbeaten 133, while Keshara Nuwantha scored 46. The pair added 112 runs for the seventh wicket.This was only the fourth time Sri Lanka had managed to save a Test after being asked to follow on.Dinusha was at the heart of Sri Lanka's resistance. He had scored 103 in the first innings of the Colombo Test and hit his maiden Test century in the series opener in Galle. His unbeaten 133 took his tally to three centuries in the two-Test series.He also became only the third batter to score centuries in both innings of a Test while following on.For India, Manav Suthar finished with 3/121 and Ravindra Jadeja took 3/94. India, however, returned home with the series win after taking the first Test in Galle.
Article Summary: Sri Lanka had lost 24 of their previous 27 Tests after being asked to follow on. Even more strikingly, they had lost all eight such Tests against India. Sri Lanka finished on 429/9 before the teams agreed to call off the match. Sonal Dinusha led the resistance with an unbeaten 133.

Article Title: FIFA World Cup’s most-hated hydration breaks could be ‘soft-launched’ in the Champions League
Article Text:
Ben Foster fears World Cup hydration breaks could eventually be trialled in the Champions League/ Image: AP

not

Why hydration breaks caused such a stir

Portugal players cool down during a hydration break during the World Cup Group K soccer match between Colombia and Portugal in Miami Gardens, Fla., Saturday, June 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Lynne Sladky)

Foster fears football is becoming ‘quarters’

Why Foster thinks the Champions League could be next

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

One of the most controversial features introduced at the 2026 World Cup could have a life beyond the tournament, with former England goalkeeper Ben Foster fearing that what began as a tournament measure could eventually become part of the regular club football landscape.Hydration breaks proved hugely unpopular with sections of supporters during the World Cup, with the three-minute stoppages midway through each half disrupting the flow of matches and prompting questions over whether football was becoming too fragmented. Foster now believes the Premier League and Champions League could eventually face the same change, although the Premier League has confirmed that it willintroduce mandatory, blanket hydration breaks among its rule changes for the 2026-27 season.FIFA introduced mandatory three-minute hydration breaks midway through each half at the World Cup, meaning matches were effectively divided into four separate periods rather than two continuous 45-minute halves.The interruptions were criticised by players and managers who felt they affected the momentum and identity of matches, with USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino making his position clear during the tournament."I don’t like it. I only like it when the conditions are extreme. But when the conditions are good, it is unnecessary," Pochettino said.The commercial side of the decision also attracted attention because broadcasters could use the stoppages as advertising opportunities. A 30-second World Cup commercial slot on Fox Sports reportedly cost between $200,000 and $300,000, with prices reaching around $750,000 during the latter stages of the competition.The World Cup final added another controversial alteration to the traditional match format. A Super Bowl-style half-time show extended the interval to 27 minutes, exceeding the 15-minute maximum stipulated by the Laws of the Game.Foster has played more than 550 professional matches for club and country, and he believes the physical impact of the stoppages could become particularly noticeable for older players because they have less time to remain loose and ready to resume at full intensity.Speaking exclusively on talkSPORT Drive, Foster said: "If you’re an older player it does, if you’re about 32 onwards [it will affect you]."I would like to think they have bikes in the changing room because they will have to get moving pretty quick, because you can stiffen up so quickly."But his concern goes beyond the physical effects. Foster believes the regular interruptions fundamentally alter how teams experience and manage a football match."The halves are not even 45 minutes anymore, they’re quarters. It would not surprise me if these hydration breaks crept into the Premier League," he said."It would not surprise me one little bit. Where there’s money to be made, there’s a way. They will find a reason to justify it." The league has confirmed That prediction is not currently reflected in the Premier League's rules for the new season.World Cup’s Most-Hated Hydration Breaks Could Be ‘Soft-Launched’ in the Champions Leaguethat mandatory hydration breaks will not be introduced across matches in 2026-27. Cooling breaks can still be used when temperatures exceed 30°C (86°F), with the referee deciding before kick-off whether conditions warrant one.Foster is nevertheless concerned that the absence of mandatory breaks in England will not necessarily stop the idea from spreading elsewhere, particularly if football discovers a financial incentive to make the interruptions part of the matchday product.He pointed to VAR as an example of how difficult it can become to reverse a change once football has invested heavily in it, regardless of how supporters feel about the system."There’s nothing we can do as football fans to stop it, they introduced VAR and every single one of us hates it," Foster said."I could do away with VAR tomorrow, but they won’t now because they invested so much money into it."He believes the Champions League could be where the concept is introduced gradually before becoming more widespread."They will do a soft launch in the Champions League, for example, you watch. Clubs will say ‘oh we get an extra million quid'."Foster also believes the World Cup breaks have already changed the way some teams approach their matches, with coaches and players able to treat each interruption almost like a reset point."Teams have been approaching games differently because it’s in quarters, so you can break it down into the four parts. But I hate it."His concerns echo those voiced by other figures in the game. England manager Thomas Tuchel has previously said the stoppages "interrupt and change the identity of a football match", while UEFA has ruled out introducing the same mandatory system in European competition.For now, then, Foster's prediction remains just that: a warning about where he believes football could be heading. The Premier League has specifically rejected mandatory hydration breaks, but his broader concern is that once a change creates a commercial opportunity, football's authorities may eventually find a reason to make it permanent.
Article Summary: Ben Foster fears World Cup hydration breaks could eventually be trialled in the Champions League. Former England goalkeeper fears that what began as a tournament measure could eventually become part of the regular club football landscape. Foster believes the regular interruptions fundamentally alter how teams experience and manage a football match. The Premier League has confirmed that it will introduce mandatory, blanket hydration break among its rule changes for the 2026-27 season.

Article Title: Free hits in Tests can fix no-ball issue: India coach
Article Text:
2nd Test: India's spin attack delivers 10 no-balls against Sri Lanka, third-highest in Tests since 2021

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India's spin bowling coach Sairaj Bahutule proposed introducing free hits in Test cricket, in half-jest, to tackle the problem of bowling no-balls after India's spinners delivered 10 no-balls in the ongoing second Test against Sri Lanka at Sinhalese Sports Club in Colombo."I am no guardian of the rules but if a free-hit comes, obviously, no-balls will definitely be reduced. No team would want to bowl those no-balls and give that extra ball and give those extra runs," said Bahutule after the fourth day's play on Wednesday.India's 10 no-balls were the most bowled by a spin attack since 2021, with Afghanistan heading the list with 14.Bahutule said the issue was being addressed within the team. "Obviously, the take-off point is talked about. They understand what is happening and definitely a process will be put forward in terms of minimising," he said.Bahutule admitted overstepping was an issue that often occurred when bowlers pushed for wickets, and said remedial work continued during India's practice sessions."It is something which we have been working on. It is definitely a concern at times. But when the bowler is putting in that effort and tries to get a wicket in situations where wickets have not been coming, he has a tendency to push himself, but that is not an excuse. A lot of work though has been put in with (Ravindra) Jadeja, with Saransh (Jain), about where the take-off point is and where it should be. But sometimes, the effort they put in for that particular delivery is a bit more and they tend to overstep. I'm sure they will rectify it and get better," the India spin bowling coach asserted.
Article Summary: Sairaj Bahutule proposes introducing free hits in Test cricket. India's spinners delivered 10 no-balls in the ongoing second Test against Sri Lanka. It was the most bowled by a spin attack since 2021, with Afghanistan heading the list with 14.

Brief scores: North Zone 251 & 222 bt West Zone 187 & 234 (overnight 220/7) all out in 57.3 overs (Abid Mushtaq 4/60, Nishant Sindhu 2/59). Semifinals lineup: North vs South; East vs Central

Bengaluru: With West Zone needing 67 runs and North Zone three wickets away from victory, both teams began the fourth and final day of their Duleep Trophy quarterfinal with a win in sight on Wednesday. North were banking on their spinners, while West hoped their capable tailenders, including Shardul Thakur, could help Urvil Patel pull off an unlikely escape at the BCCI Centre of Excellence here.But it took North just 28 minutes to wrap up West, adding only 14 runs to their overnight total of 220 and securing a semifinal date with South Zone, starting Aug 30.Jammu & Kashmir left-arm spinner Abid Mushtaq, who finished with a match haul of nine wickets, uprooted Tanush Kotian's middle stump in the second over to set the wheels in motion. Bowling with accuracy and a flatter trajectory, Abid then had Tushar Deshpande caught sharply at first slip by Abdul Samad.Fellow spinner Nishant Sindhu trapped Urvil leg before wicket to bring the match to an end. Shardul, who walked in at No. 11, did not even face a ball.West had lost the plot late on Tuesday, collapsing from 209/3 to 234 all out as they lost four wickets for 25 runs. Before the late collapse, North Zone left-arm seamer Arshdeep Singh was already looking forward to returning to Punjab. "I was thinking about 'Sher-e-Punjab', going back home, and what time ticket should I book!" said Arshdeep, who claimed four wickets in the match.
Article Summary: North Zone beat West Zone by three wickets in Duleep Trophy quarterfinal. North set up semifinal against South Zone, starting Aug 30. West Zone lost four wickets for 25 runs late on Tuesday, collapsing from 209/3 to 234 all out.

Article Title: Asian Games: Questions over selections across squads
Article Text:
Protistha Samanta competes on the floor exercise during the women's team final and individual qualification of Artistic Gymnastics at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, Saturday, July 25, 2026. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Complaint over failure to get horse-owner accreditation:

NEW DELHI: India's Asian Games squads are facing fresh selection scrutiny with questions being raised over the criteria used in gymnastics, kurash and karate.In gymnastics, Pranati Nayak is the lone athlete to be cleared. There is no explanation on why other gymnasts who earned nominative, by-name quotas from the Asian Gymnastics Union (AGU) were not considered.Following the 2026 Asian Championships, Nishka Agarwal earned a nominative all-around qualification while Pranati and Protistha Samanta secured nominative qualification as vault specialists. The 2025 Asian meet adds context - Pranati won bronze while Protishta finished fourth.The 2026 championships, held after June 20, fell outside the ministry's qualification window. But if the 2025 Asian event was used as criteria, then Protishta, too, should have made the cut.Protishta had India's best gymnastics result at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, finishing seventh and becoming the only Indian gymnast to reach the final. Pranati competed there injured and could not make the final cut. "The question is whether the framework was applied consistently for the Asian Games.If yes, then on that basis, Protishta and Nishka, along with men's gymnasts Tapan Mohanty and Yogeshwar Singh, also deserved consideration," said federation sources.Kurash raises another question. India returned from the Hangzhou Games without a medal, yet a six-member team has been cleared after an initial decision by authorities not to send one. With no performance benchmark cited, the selection remains unclear.Karate is equally perplexing. SAI had formed a committee and initially decided not to send a team, according to sources. Yet Alisha Choudhary and Chetan Bhatt have been named. The IOA barred the Karate India Organisation (KIO) from functioning as an NSF over unauthorised selection and otherviolations.Dressage rider Shruti Vora has written to IOA president PT Usha seeking urgent intervention in securing the crucial horse-owner accreditation and blaming the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI) for oversight.
Article Summary: Questions being raised over the criteria used in gymnastics, kurash and karate. Pranati Nayak is the lone athlete to be cleared. There is no explanation on why other gymnasts who earned nominative, by-name quotas from the Asian Gymnastics Union were not considered.

Article Title: Dressage rider Shruti Vora seeks IOA intervention over alleged EFI lapse in horse owner accreditation for Asian Games
Article Text:
Shruti Vora

NEW DELHI: Indian dressage rider Shruti Vora has sought the immediate intervention of the Indian Olympic Association (IOA), alleging that the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI) failed to process horse owner accreditation for the Asian Games despite receiving the required documents nearly two months before the deadline.In a letter addressed to the IOA, a copy of which is with TOI, Shruti, a member of the Indian dressage team for the Asian Games, alleged that all required horse owner details, duly notarised, were submitted to the EFI on June 3. According to her, neither she nor fellow athletes received an acknowledgement or response from the federation despite repeated follow-ups on July 13, 17, 19 and 30.Shruti has alleged that the EFI raised the issue with the Asian Games Organising Committee in Japan only on July 29 — nearly two months after receiving the documentation from the athletes. Further reminders were sent by athletes on August 2 and 3, she said.The matter, according to Shruti's letter, took a more serious turn on August 14, when the Asian Games Organising Committee informed the EFI that while FEI regulations permit two horse owner accreditations or passes per horse, the names of the horse owners were required to have been submitted along with the Definite Entries.Shruti has alleged that the delay by the EFI has consequently left horse owners at risk of being denied accreditation, despite the athletes having submitted the required information well in advance."This is not an unavoidable administrative issue," Shruti alleged in her communication to the IOA, describing the situation as a consequence of what she termed a "serious failure" by the federation to act on documentation submitted in time.The dressage rider also questioned whether athletes' interests and essential administrative requirements were being handled with the seriousness expected of a national sports federation representing India at the Asian Games.For equestrian athletes, horse owners and support personnel can play an important role during major international competitions, and Shruti argued that athletes should not be made to bear the consequences of an administrative delay when they had completed the required formalities within the stipulated time.Shruti has now requested the IOA to intervene with the EFI and the Asian Games Organising Committee and ensure that the horse owner accreditations are processed as originally requested.She has also sought written confirmation of the resolution, stressing that the matter is "urgent and time sensitive" with the Games approaching.The rider said repeated attempts by athletes to resolve the matter directly with the EFI had allegedly resulted in neither timely action nor meaningful communication, prompting them to seek IOA intervention.Shruti's letter is an allegation from the athlete's side, and the claims regarding the EFI's handling of the accreditation process have not been independently established. The EFI's response to the allegations was not included in the communication shared by Shruti.The Asian Games 2026 are scheduled to be held in Japan, with the Indian equestrian contingent preparing for the continental multi-sport event. Shruti has urged the IOA to ensure that athletes are not prejudiced by what she alleges are administrative failures beyond their control.
Article Summary: Dressage rider Shruti Vora alleges that the Equestrian Federation of India failed to process horse owner accreditation for the Asian Games. Vora claims that all required horse owner details, duly notarised, were submitted to the EFI on June 3. She alleges that neither she nor fellow athletes received an acknowledgement or response from the federation despite repeated follow-ups.

Article Title: 'Big shock for all of us': Savita Punia urges Hockey India to keep league alive as Women’s HIL faces uncertain future
Article Text:

KOLKATA: Despite the good showing by the Indian women’s hockey team at the ongoing World Cup, the players were in for a rude shock when they learnt about the concerns surrounding the next edition of the Women’s Hockey India League.Reacting to the news, former India captain and one of the highest-capped player, Savita Punia, told TOI on Wednesday, “Ever since we came to know that teams in the women’s league are considering pulling out, it has definitely been a big shock for all of us. We had been looking forward to the league because we felt it would give us good exposure, especially our young players.”Of the four teams that competed last year, two are considering pulling out while another remains undecided. SG Pipers won the tournament last year, while Shrachi Bengal Tigers clinched the title the year before.“Financially, the league definitely helps, but more importantly, it gives you a platform to train and share your experiences with some of the best players in the world,” added Savita. “There are so many players who dream of doing something for India in hockey, and HIL is one of the best platforms to help them achieve that.”According to one franchise owner, whose team incurred losses running into crores over the two seasons, the biggest reason for considering a pullout was Hockey India’s failure to raise funds as promised.“The tournament isn’t financially viable and that is the only reason for deciding to pull out,” said the owner, who has teams in both the men’s and women’s tournaments.Another franchise official, however, played down those concerns, pointing out that with franchise fees being scrapped from the next edition onwards, and each owner required to pay only Rs 1 crore each for a men’s and women’s team, two teams can now be run at a minimum cost of around Rs 12.5 crore.“Considering that this is only a two-year-old tournament, this should not be a major concern,” the franchise official said.It is understood that Hockey India president Dilip Tirkey, who did not travel to the World Cup unlike several other HI officials, is making efforts to ensure that the tournament goes ahead as planned. He also held meetings with various stakeholders to address the concerns surrounding the league.There had also been discussions about appointing a dedicated sponsorship professional for the HIL, effectively in the role of a director, to drive revenue and commercial partnerships. However, the proposal is understood to have run into differences over remuneration and the reporting structure.While the franchises and Hockey India continue to work through the financial and structural concerns, the players are hoping that a solution is found soon, given the league’s importance to the growth of women’s hockey in the country.“The Indian women’s team is working very hard to take Indian hockey forward, and the HIL is a very big supporter of that journey. So, on behalf of all of us and the women’s team, I would request that the HIL should continue,” Savita further added.With the next edition still facing uncertainty, the coming weeks could prove crucial for the future of the women’s HIL and the opportunities it provides to India’s emerging players.
Article Summary: Women's Hockey India League facing financial and structural concerns. Two teams are considering pulling out while another remains undecided. SG Pipers won the tournament last year, while Shrachi Bengal Tigers clinched the title the year before. Hockey India president Dilip Tirkey is making efforts to ensure that the tournament goes ahead as planned.

Article Title: 'Played competitive matches against boys': Pakistan skipper Fatima Sana reveals unusual Asia Cup preparation

Pakistan’s women’s cricket team have taken an unusual route to prepare for the Women’s Asia Cup, playing full T20 matches against a men’s side during their training camp in Lahore.The matches against the Abdul Qadir Cricket Academy featured both teenage and senior male players.Unlike regular practice sessions, the games were played under full Twenty20 rules, with Pakistan aiming to expose their players to greater pressure and improve their decision-making in difficult situations.Pakistan have never won the Women’s Asia Cup. Their best performances came in 2012 and 2016, when they reached the final but lost to India on both occasions. They have not reached the final since and were eliminated in the semi-finals in the previous two editions.Captain Fatima Sana believes the matches against the men will help the team deal with pressure better.“We are well prepared for the tournament,” Fatima said, as quoted by Cricinfo. “We have played competitive matches against boys in which we were put under pressure. These learnings will help us adapt to the challenges of the competition.”Pakistan enter the tournament after a poor T20 World Cup campaign, winning only one of their five matches. Fatima was among their standout performers, scoring an unbeaten 55 against South Africa and taking 11 wickets, the second-highest tally in the tournament.The captain said dealing with pressure was a major focus during the team’s preparations.“We needed to understand how to handle the pressure better, and that is something which is highlighted whenever there is a big tournament,” she said. “These matches have helped us on that front, and the difference will be visible.“It is very important to stay calm in pressure situations rather than pressing the panic button. We have told the girls to stay calm in the crunch moments, stay in control, trust their hard work and execute the plans.”Fatima will return for the Asia Cup after missing Pakistan’s recent Sri Lanka series while playing in The Hundred.Pakistan are in Group A with India, Thailand and Hong Kong. They begin against Thailand on September 1, face India on September 5 and play Hong Kong on September 7.

The matches against the Abdul Qadir Cricket Academy featured both teenage and senior male players. Captain Fatima Sana believes the matches will help the team deal with pressure better.

Article Title: 'People will lose interest in Pakistan cricket': Moin Khan slams PCB, selectors
Article Text:
Pakistan head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and Babar Azam (AFP Photo)

'People will lose interest in Pakistan cricket '

Frequent changes hurting Pakistan cricket

Moin questions players' priorities

'Priorities have changed'

Concern over Pakistan's pace bowling

NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan captain Moin Khan has warned that the country could find it increasingly difficult to arrange bilateral series with top teams if the national side continues to struggle. Moin, who played 69 Tests and 219 ODIs for Pakistan, also criticised the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) and the national selectors for the way the cricket system has been handled in recent years.Moin said Pakistan have struggled across formats, particularly in Test cricket. He fears the situation could get worse if the team's poor results continue."We have been struggling in all formats but notably in test matches and if this trend continues I am afraid people will lose interest in Pakistan cricket," Moin said on a podcast.He warned that Pakistan could slip down the cricketing order and face problems in attracting top teams for bilateral series."We might find ourselves relegated to the bottom half of the cricket world finding it difficult to get bilateral series with top teams."I blame the frequent changes being made by the board in the cricket system including appointments/removal of captains, coaches, players and the inexplicable calls made by the national selectors."Unless you don’t have continuity, stability and faith in a captain, coach or players, how can you expect to achieve good results," he said.Moin said repeated changes in domestic cricket and the national team have affected Pakistan badly. According to him, the uncertainty has also resulted in players losing confidence in the system.The former wicketkeeper-batter also said the PCB often makes decisions based on the people in power at a particular time rather than following a consistent institutional approach."Whenever a chairman and management team is changed you see things change in our cricket system which are not necessarily productive. So where is the stability?," he asked.Moin also held some of the players responsible for the current situation. He expressed disappointment with the approach of players who, according to him, are not spending enough time improving their skills and cricketing temperament."I don’t want to harp on the past but to me it seems most players nowadays don’t give enough time to developing their skills and cricket temperament. It is more about how much money we can make in leagues rather than setting and reaching personal goals of excellence as a cricketer.”He said financial rewards would follow if a player first focused on performing successfully for the national team."When I played we earned in lakhs. Nowadays players earn in crores but players must also remember nothing is greater than playing for your country with success."Moin said he had given similar advice to his son, Azam Khan, who has played T20 internationals for Pakistan. He said representing the country should take priority over private leagues."I guess priorities have changed for players now. The PCB and selectors have not helped by devaluing the Pakistan cap,” he added.According to Moin, playing for Pakistan in his time required considerable hard work, sacrifice and preparation.He recalled how preparation helped him perform under pressure."People ask me how you always got runs in a crisis situation and I tell them it is all about how well you prepare as a player for the matches."Moin also expressed concern about the current state of pace bowling in Pakistan. He said bowlers need to put in more hours to develop their skills and improve their pace."Bowlers are not willing to put in the hours. I played with greats like Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis , Shoaib Akhtar and I can tell you the perfection of bowling on any sort of pitch and increased pace only comes when you put in long hours in the nets.”Moin said the great fast bowlers he played alongside worked extremely hard on their skills and fitness. He made it clear all these greats worked very hard on their skills and fitness by themselves.
Article Summary: Former Pakistan captain Moin Khan has warned that the country could find it increasingly difficult to arrange bilateral series with top teams. Moin, who played 69 Tests and 219 ODIs for Pakistan, also criticised the Pakistan Cricket Board and the national selectors for the way the cricket system has been handled.

Sonal Dinusha stood tall for Sri Lanka and scored a defiant century to keep India at bay on Day 5 of the second Test in Colombo.Dinusha was unbeaten on 98 at tea and did not have to wait long to complete his century. On the first ball of the third and final session, he flicked Mohammed Siraj towards mid-wicket for a couple of runs to reach the landmark.It was another brilliant innings from the Sri Lankan batter, who continued his sublime run in the two-match Test series against India.Dinusha had already scored a century in the first Test in Galle, where Sri Lanka suffered a 165-run defeat. He continued his fine form in the second Test, scoring 103 runs in the first innings. With Sri Lanka under pressure to save the Test and avoid a 2-0 series whitewash, Dinusha once again rose to the occasion and scored another hundred.His latest century gave him three hundreds in the two-match series. He became only the third Sri Lankan batter to score three centuries in a two-match Test series.He also joined an elite group of batters who have scored three hundreds in a two-Test series. Dinusha is now one of nine players to achieve the feat.Overall, Dinusha became the 12th batter to score centuries in both innings of a Test against India. More importantly, he is only the second batter to achieve the feat against India since January 2015. The previous batter to do so was England's Jonny Bairstow, who scored 106 and an unbeaten 114 against India at Edgbaston in 2022.Dinusha's 103 in the first innings and unbeaten 100 in the second innings have now put him in that elite group. Third Sri Lankan to achieve the feat against IndiaDinusha also became only the third Sri Lankan batter to score centuries in both innings of a Test against India. Duleep Mendis was the first Sri Lankan to do it, scoring 105 in both innings against India in Chennai in 1982. Aravinda de Silva was the second. He scored 146 and 120 at the Colombo SSC against India in 1997.Now, Dinusha has become the third Sri Lankan to join the list. His scores of 103 and 100 not out came at the Colombo SSC in 2026.Aravinda de Silva is the only player to feature twice on the list. He scored three centuries against Pakistan at home in 1997 and repeated the feat against India at home later that year. South Africa's Jacques Kallis scored three hundreds against Pakistan away from home in 2007, while Hashim Amla scored three against India away from home in 2010.Kumar Sangakkara scored three centuries for Sri Lanka against Bangladesh at home in 2013. Pakistan's Younis Khan then scored three hundreds against Australia at a neutral venue in 2014.Australia's Marnus Labuschagne scored three centuries against West Indies at home in 2022, while New Zealand's Kane Williamson did the same against South Africa at home in 2024.Dinusha is the latest name on the list after scoring three hundreds against India at home in 2026.Dinusha's 103 in the first innings and his unbeaten 100 in the second innings also helped him achieve another major feat. He became the eighth Sri Lankan batter to score centuries in both innings of a Test.Aravinda de Silva and Kumar Sangakkara are the only two players on the list to have achieved the feat twice. The other Sri Lankan batters to do it are Duleep Mendis, Asanka Gurusinha, Tillakaratne Dilshan, Dhananjaya de Silva and Kamindu Mendis.The list shows how rare Dinusha's achievement is. Several great Sri Lankan batters, including Sangakkara and Aravinda, have achieved it, while only eight Sri Lankan players have managed to score a century in both innings of a Test.
Article Summary: Sonal Dinusha scored a defiant century to keep India at bay on Day 5 of the second Test in Colombo. Dinusha had already scored a century in the first Test in Galle, where Sri Lanka suffered a 165-run defeat. His latest century gave him three hundreds in the two-match series. He became only the third Sri Lankan batter to score three centuries in a two- match Test series.

Article Title: ‘It’s my opinion’: AB de Villiers hits back after Virat Kohli-Sachin Tendulkar comparison sparks backlash
Article Text:
AB de Villiers on Virat Kohli-Sachin Tendulkar

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

South Africa great AB de Villiers has clarified his recent comments comparing Virat Kohli with Sachin Tendulkar after his assessment of the two Indian batting legends triggered a backlash on social media.De Villiers had previously said Kohli was better than Tendulkar in seam-friendly overseas conditions, while crediting the former India opener with being the first Indian batter to show that players from the subcontinent could succeed consistently in challenging conditions outside Asia.The former South Africa captain's comments attracted criticism, prompting him to explain what he meant.“There was a bit of confusion with my Virat and Sachin comment. Remember, it's my opinion. I'm not axing anyone. I'm telling you the way that I see it. Sachin was the first to take things forward for India, showing all the youngsters what it takes to perform consistently everywhere around the world. I said that Virat sort of showed that there is a different dynamic to Indian batting by being good on the short ball. He found a way to counter that,” de Villiers said on his YouTube channel.De Villiers acknowledged that Kohli's overseas numbers do not match Tendulkar's, but insisted that statistics alone do not determine how he assesses a batter.“We can always look at stats and say Virat's stats were not as good abroad, especially because of England, where he really struggled. But I still feel he looked confident and played the all-round, well-balanced cricket that's needed to succeed abroad and inspired a lot of youngsters around him. He took what he learnt from Sachin and took it forward. His record is not as good as Sachin's away from home, but we don't always look at stats, especially not me. And that's what I meant with showing the new generation of cricketers how the way forward should look. Staying fit, leading by example, having the all-round game,” de Villiers concluded.His original assessment had centred on how Kohli built on Tendulkar's pioneering work.“I think of someone like Sachin Tendulkar way back, who started that trend for India. Yet, he wasn't as strong as someone like Virat Kohli, who was even better. But Sachin was the first guy to show that, as a subcontinent batter, you can do well in bouncy and seaming conditions. Virat took that forward and raised the bar. Because of that, there are quite a few players now like Rahul and Padikkal, who have started to up that trend and follow in the footsteps of a Virat and a Sachin,” de Villiers had stated earlier.The statistical comparison, however, strongly favours Tendulkar in overseas Tests.Tendulkar remains the leading run-scorer in Test history, having accumulated 15,921 runs in 200 matches before retiring in 2013. Kohli retired from Test cricket in May 2025 after scoring 9,230 runs in 123 Tests, leaving him 19th on the all-time list.Tendulkar scored 8,705 of his Test runs away from home, accounting for around 55% of his career tally. He is also the highest run-scorer in overseas Test cricket. Kohli, meanwhile, made 4,774 runs in 66 Tests outside India.The difference remains significant when the comparison is restricted to SENA nations. Tendulkar scored 5,387 runs in 63 Tests in South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia at an average of 51.30, including 17 centuries and 23 fifties.Kohli finished with 3,661 runs in 46 Tests across the same countries at an average of 42.08, with 12 centuries and 14 fifties.De Villiers' clarification therefore sought to put his original comments into context, with the South African stressing that his assessment was based not merely on numbers but on Kohli's approach, adaptability, fitness and influence on the generation that followed him.
Article Summary: AB de Villiers has clarified his comments comparing Virat Kohli with Sachin Tendulkar. The South African had previously said Kohli was better in overseas conditions. His comments attracted a backlash on social media, prompting him to explain what he meant.

NEW DELHI: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey, with the state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house.The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal.Dey won the women’s -48kg title in Glasgow after defeating Canada’s Heidi Quach in a dramatic golden-score contest. The state government also presented her with a cheque of Rs 10 lakh as part of the felicitation.Speaking at the event, Saha highlighted Dey’s difficult journey from a small village in South Tripura to the top of the Commonwealth Games podium. Her father, he noted, worked as a cycle mechanic in Sonaichari.“The journey from an obscure village in South Tripura to a podium finish at Glasgow was a race against time. Her father was a cycle mechanic at Sonaichari. Against all odds, she stood firm on her mission and achieved phenomenal success for the country,” he said.The chief minister recalled meeting Dey at Tripura Bhavan in New Delhi after her return from the Games.During that meeting, the judoka had expressed her wish to have a house in Agartala.“During the meeting, Asmita revealed she desperately wanted a house in Agartala. I promised to fulfil her wish, and today a piece of land has been allotted to her,” he said.Saha said Dey’s achievement could motivate more young athletes from Tripura to pursue sport at the highest level. He also urged her to remain disciplined as she prepares for the Asian Games, particularly because of the strict anti-doping requirements.“I urge Asmita to remain alert, particularly about food, because she has to pass through a stringent dope test before joining the prestigious Asian Games. We believe she will shine again in the Asian Games by winning a medal for the country,” he said.Youth Affairs and Sports Minister Tinku Roy, Agartala Mayor Dipak Majumder and Arjuna award-winning gymnast Dipa Karmakar were among those who attended the felicitation ceremony.
Article Summary: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey. The state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house. The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth games gold medal.

Article Title: Rajasthan stuck in 2012, Manipur in 2023: How actively are states with CWG medals promoting sports?
Article Text:
Are sports bodies of Indian states promoting the game properly?

Medal tally of India's athletes by birth state/UT

Haryana: Hit on the podium, not so much off it

Manipur still talking about 2023

Rajasthan: 14 years and counting

Uttar Pradesh and Delhi carry the same gloomy picture

And then come Tamil Nadu and others

The ones somewhere in the middle

How active are states/UTs with CWG medallists in promoting sport

Does it matter so much?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Social media presence Local sports events Government funding 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi interacted with India's CWG 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday. (Pic credit: PM Modi's X post)

Mirabai recalls four years of struggle

‘One family will bring three medals’

India’s Glasgow success

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hosted medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg. Modi heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.
